title: Inheritance, virtual dispatch and abstract classes
body: A derived class inherits the members of its base class: `class Circle : Shape`. C# supports single class inheritance (one base class) and multiple interface implementation. Constructors are not inherited; a derived constructor chains to a base constructor with `: base(...)`, and the base part is initialized first.

A `virtual` member can be replaced with `override` in a derived class. Calls through a base-typed reference dispatch to the most derived override at runtime: `Shape s = new Circle(1); s.Area()` runs `Circle.Area`. That runtime choice is polymorphism. `base.Describe()` calls the base implementation from inside an override.

An `abstract` class cannot be instantiated and may declare `abstract` members with no body that every concrete derived class must override. Use it when derived types share state or implementation. `sealed` on a class prevents further derivation; on an override it stops deeper overrides.

Declaring a member with the same name but without `override` hides the base member (the compiler warns CS0114 or CS0108; use `new` to say it is deliberate). Hidden members are chosen by the static type of the reference, not the runtime type, which surprises readers. Prefer override.

Calling a virtual method from a base constructor runs the derived override before the derived constructor has initialized its fields. Before designing a hierarchy, check whether composition or an interface would be simpler, and mark classes `sealed` unless they are designed for inheritance.

challenge: Add an abstract Employee class with an abstract MonthlyPay() and a virtual Title, then Salaried(decimal annual) and Hourly(decimal rate, int hours) subclasses. Print the total pay for one of each.
question: Given `Shape s = new Circle();` and a virtual Area overridden in Circle, which Area runs for `s.Area()`?
wrong: Shape.Area, because s is declared as Shape
Whichever was declared last in the file
reasoning: virtual/override dispatches on the runtime type; only hiding with new uses the static type.
